# Importance, effect size, marginal effects and SHAP

## There is no single universal definition of importance

Researchers often ask which predictor is “most important”. That question
is underspecified. A large standardized slope, a large unique
contribution to `R-squared`, a high LMG decomposition and a large
average absolute SHAP value can rank variables differently because they
describe different properties of the fitted model.

This vignette keeps these meanings separate.

## Soil-fertility model

``` r

soil <- mr_example_data("soil_fertility")
fit <- mr_fit(
  yield_t_ha ~ soil_pH + organic_matter_pct + clay_pct +
    available_P_mg_dm3 + exchangeable_K_mg_dm3 +
    soil_moisture_pct + season_rain_mm,
  soil
)
```

## Example 1: standardized coefficients

``` r

std <- mr_importance(fit, "standardized")
std[order(-abs(std$standardized_beta)), ]
#>                    term standardized_beta
#> 7        season_rain_mm        0.38835898
#> 4    available_P_mg_dm3        0.34510847
#> 5 exchangeable_K_mg_dm3        0.33206057
#> 2    organic_matter_pct        0.16713549
#> 6     soil_moisture_pct        0.14200401
#> 1               soil_pH       -0.03219004
#> 3              clay_pct       -0.03168960
```

A standardized coefficient expresses the conditional slope after scaling
the predictor and response by their standard deviations. It is still a
coefficient from the specified regression model and remains sensitive to
collinearity.

## Example 2: partial R-squared

``` r

pr2 <- mr_importance(fit, "partial_r2")
pr2[order(-pr2$partial_R2), ]
#>                    term  partial_R2
#> 7        season_rain_mm 0.201508234
#> 4    available_P_mg_dm3 0.168171187
#> 5 exchangeable_K_mg_dm3 0.153984195
#> 2    organic_matter_pct 0.045144609
#> 6     soil_moisture_pct 0.032842003
#> 1               soil_pH 0.001666390
#> 3              clay_pct 0.001603957
```

For a one-degree-of-freedom coefficient, partial R-squared describes the
fraction of residual variation associated with that coefficient after
accounting for the remaining model. It is closely related to the
coefficient t statistic.

## Example 3: semi-partial R-squared

``` r

spr2 <- mr_importance(fit, "semi_partial_r2")
spr2[order(-spr2$semi_partial_R2), ]
#>                    term semi_partial_R2
#> 7        season_rain_mm    0.1468327939
#> 4    available_P_mg_dm3    0.1176300654
#> 5 exchangeable_K_mg_dm3    0.1059005899
#> 2    organic_matter_pct    0.0275086322
#> 6     soil_moisture_pct    0.0197575420
#> 1               soil_pH    0.0009711845
#> 3              clay_pct    0.0009347394
```

Semi-partial R-squared measures the reduction in total response
variation when a term is added to a model that already contains the
other terms. Because it uses term-level deletion, it is useful for
multi-degree-of-freedom terms as well as simple slopes.

## LMG relative importance

``` r

if (requireNamespace("relaimpo", quietly = TRUE)) {
  lmg <- mr_importance(fit, "lmg")
  lmg$lmg
}
#>               soil_pH    organic_matter_pct              clay_pct 
#>           0.001812739           0.069128532           0.003421464 
#>    available_P_mg_dm3 exchangeable_K_mg_dm3     soil_moisture_pct 
#>           0.268276694           0.266684064           0.046873903 
#>        season_rain_mm 
#>           0.343802603
```

LMG averages the incremental contribution to `R-squared` over predictor
orderings. It is especially useful when predictors share explained
variation. It remains a descriptive decomposition of model fit rather
than a causal ranking.

## SHAP for the additive linear model

``` r

if (requireNamespace("kernelshap", quietly = TRUE)) {
  sh <- mr_importance(fit, "shap")
  head(sh$S)
  sort(colMeans(abs(sh$S)), decreasing = TRUE)
}
#> Exact additive SHAP via predict(..., type = 'terms')
#>        season_rain_mm    available_P_mg_dm3 exchangeable_K_mg_dm3 
#>            0.23268189            0.19227006            0.19089483 
#>    organic_matter_pct     soil_moisture_pct               soil_pH 
#>            0.09934998            0.08410735            0.01921310 
#>              clay_pct 
#>            0.01916650
```

For an additive linear model, the package delegates to the efficient
additive SHAP route. Model-agnostic Kernel SHAP would be unnecessarily
expensive here. SHAP contributions describe model predictions relative
to a baseline. A large SHAP value does not establish that changing the
predictor will cause the predicted response to change by the same
amount.

## Marginal effects: soil example

``` r

if (requireNamespace("marginaleffects", quietly = TRUE)) {
  mr_effects(fit, variables = "available_P_mg_dm3")
}
#> 
#>  Estimate Std. Error   z Pr(>|z|)    S  2.5 % 97.5 %
#>    0.0273    0.00462 5.9   <0.001 28.0 0.0182 0.0363
#> 
#> Term: available_P_mg_dm3
#> Type: response
#> Comparison: dY/dX
```

## Marginal effects: rainfall example

``` r

if (requireNamespace("marginaleffects", quietly = TRUE)) {
  mr_effects(fit, variables = "season_rain_mm")
}
#> 
#>  Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)    S   2.5 %  97.5 %
#>   0.00326   0.000495 6.59   <0.001 34.4 0.00229 0.00423
#> 
#> Term: season_rain_mm
#> Type: response
#> Comparison: dY/dX
```

## Marginal effects: plant-science example

``` r

plant <- mr_example_data("plant_growth")
fit_plant <- mr_fit(
  biomass_g ~ leaf_area_cm2 + chlorophyll_spad + leaf_N_pct +
    stomatal_conductance + plant_height_cm + root_mass_g,
  plant
)
if (requireNamespace("marginaleffects", quietly = TRUE)) {
  mr_effects(fit_plant, variables = c("leaf_N_pct", "chlorophyll_spad"))
}
#> 
#>              Term Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)    S 2.5 % 97.5 %
#>  chlorophyll_spad    0.177     0.0178 9.95   <0.001 75.1 0.142  0.212
#>  leaf_N_pct          1.477     0.2397 6.16   <0.001 30.4 1.007  1.947
#> 
#> Type: response
#> Comparison: dY/dX
```

For a purely additive linear model, average slopes equal the
corresponding coefficients. The distinction becomes more valuable for
interactions and nonlinear models.

## Interaction example

``` r

fit_int <- mr_fit(
  yield_t_ha ~ available_P_mg_dm3 * soil_moisture_pct +
    organic_matter_pct + season_rain_mm,
  soil
)
summary(fit_int)
#> 
#> Call:
#> (function (formula, data, subset, weights, na.action, method = "qr", 
#>     model = TRUE, x = FALSE, y = FALSE, qr = TRUE, singular.ok = TRUE, 
#>     contrasts = NULL, offset, ...) 
#> {
#>     ret.x <- x
#>     ret.y <- y
#>     cl <- match.call()
#>     mf <- match.call(expand.dots = FALSE)
#>     m <- match(c("formula", "data", "subset", "weights", "na.action", 
#>         "offset"), names(mf), 0L)
#>     mf <- mf[c(1L, m)]
#>     mf$drop.unused.levels <- TRUE
#>     mf[[1L]] <- quote(stats::model.frame)
#>     mf <- eval(mf, parent.frame())
#>     if (method == "model.frame") 
#>         return(mf)
#>     else if (method != "qr") 
#>         warning(gettextf("method = '%s' is not supported. Using 'qr'", 
#>             method), domain = NA)
#>     mt <- attr(mf, "terms")
#>     y <- model.response(mf, "numeric")
#>     w <- as.vector(model.weights(mf))
#>     if (!is.null(w) && !is.numeric(w)) 
#>         stop("'weights' must be a numeric vector")
#>     offset <- model.offset(mf)
#>     mlm <- is.matrix(y)
#>     ny <- if (mlm) 
#>         nrow(y)
#>     else length(y)
#>     if (!is.null(offset)) {
#>         if (!mlm) 
#>             offset <- as.vector(offset)
#>         if (NROW(offset) != ny) 
#>             stop(gettextf("number of offsets is %d, should equal %d (number of observations)", 
#>                 NROW(offset), ny), domain = NA)
#>     }
#>     if (is.empty.model(mt)) {
#>         x <- NULL
#>         z <- list(coefficients = if (mlm) matrix(NA_real_, 0, 
#>             ncol(y)) else numeric(), residuals = y, fitted.values = 0 * 
#>             y, weights = w, rank = 0L, df.residual = if (!is.null(w)) sum(w != 
#>             0) else ny)
#>         if (!is.null(offset)) {
#>             z$fitted.values <- offset
#>             z$residuals <- y - offset
#>         }
#>     }
#>     else {
#>         x <- model.matrix(mt, mf, contrasts)
#>         z <- if (is.null(w)) 
#>             lm.fit(x, y, offset = offset, singular.ok = singular.ok, 
#>                 ...)
#>         else lm.wfit(x, y, w, offset = offset, singular.ok = singular.ok, 
#>             ...)
#>     }
#>     class(z) <- c(if (mlm) "mlm", "lm")
#>     z$na.action <- attr(mf, "na.action")
#>     z$offset <- offset
#>     z$contrasts <- attr(x, "contrasts")
#>     z$xlevels <- .getXlevels(mt, mf)
#>     z$call <- cl
#>     z$terms <- mt
#>     if (model) 
#>         z$model <- mf
#>     if (ret.x) 
#>         z$x <- x
#>     if (ret.y) 
#>         z$y <- y
#>     if (!qr) 
#>         z$qr <- NULL

#> })(formula = yield_t_ha ~ available_P_mg_dm3 * soil_moisture_pct +

```

With an interaction, the coefficient of available P no longer represents
one constant P effect across all soil moisture levels. Marginal-effect
tools can summarize the average slope or evaluate the slope at
meaningful moisture values.

``` r

if (requireNamespace("marginaleffects", quietly = TRUE)) {
  mr_effects(fit_int, variables = "available_P_mg_dm3")
}
#> 
#>  Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)    S 2.5 % 97.5 %
#>     0.027    0.00512 5.28   <0.001 22.9 0.017 0.0371
#> 
#> Term: available_P_mg_dm3
#> Type: response
#> Comparison: dY/dX
```

## Compare importance under collinearity

``` r

coll <- mr_example_data("agronomy_collinear")
fit_coll <- mr_fit(yield_t_ha ~ ., coll)
mr_importance(fit_coll, "standardized")
#>                   term standardized_beta
#> 1         N_rate_kg_ha        0.53571374
#> 2       N_uptake_kg_ha       -0.03307519
#> 3        canopy_N_g_m2        0.05102155
#> 4                 NDVI        0.05026329
#> 5       season_rain_mm        0.38360424
#> 6 soil_mineral_N_mg_kg        0.47514661
mr_importance(fit_coll, "semi_partial_r2")
#>                   term semi_partial_R2
#> 1         N_rate_kg_ha    0.0250649270
#> 2       N_uptake_kg_ha    0.0001289263
#> 3        canopy_N_g_m2    0.0015243532
#> 4                 NDVI    0.0007021686
#> 5       season_rain_mm    0.1423283625
#> 6 soil_mineral_N_mg_kg    0.2203897949
```

Under strong collinearity, unique-contribution measures can become small
even when a group of predictors jointly carries substantial information.
This is one reason not to interpret importance rankings without the
collinearity analysis.

## Reporting recommendations

State exactly which definition of importance is used. Report uncertainty
where available. Avoid phrases such as “X caused most of the yield
variation” when the analysis only supports a model-based descriptive
ranking. When predictors have different units or belong to correlated
groups, show more than one importance view and explain why rankings
differ.
